title: Capulin Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Capulin wells have a median depth of 86 feet; see local yields, water levels, drillers, and estimated well costs.
h1: What Capulin Wells Cost and How Much Water They Make
intro_html:
Buying land around Capulin means looking past the asking price and checking the well record. Within 5 miles, Colorado DWR records show 581 permitted wells, with 400 recorded as constructed. Of those, 387 report a total depth and 87 report a pump yield, so the local data is useful but not complete.

Capulin sits near La Jara, Romeo, and the San Luis Valley’s wider agricultural area. Records identify both alluvial valley aquifers and unnamed or fractured-bedrock sources. That combination can make one parcel straightforward and the next one less predictable. Neighboring well permits, the intended use, and the site’s access for drilling all belong in your due diligence.

sections.heading: Capulin well depths vary more than the median suggests
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Capulin is 86 feet. The middle half runs from 54 to 198 feet, which is the range a buyer is most likely to see in ordinary local records, but it is not a guarantee for a new hole. Fifty-four percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 29% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Fourteen percent are 300 to 600 feet, and 3% are deeper than 600 feet.

The deepest well on record reaches 1,044 feet. For a driller’s bid, the median is a useful starting point, not a fixed target. A parcel over valley alluvium may differ from one drawing water in fractured bedrock. Review nearby completed wells before assuming the 86-foot figure applies to your lot.

sections.heading: Local well yields are generally workable, but records are limited
sections.html:
Among the 87 Capulin-area wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 13.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-eight percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, and 46% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Five percent fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while 1% report under 1 gallon per minute.

That distribution is encouraging for ordinary household use, but it does not tell you the yield of an untested property. Ask for the well construction report and pumping information, not just a verbal claim. A low-producing well can still work with storage and careful demand management; a high reported yield does not replace a current inspection and water test.

sections.heading: Water levels show a deeper recent measurement pattern
sections.html:
The reported static water level has a median depth of 51 feet below the surface. The middle half ranges from 16 to 167 feet, showing substantial variation from well to well. Only 28 records report a static water level, so this is a smaller sample than the depth information.

By measurement decade, the median was 14 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 62 feet in the 2020s. That change suggests deeper measured water levels in the more recent records, but it does not by itself prove that the regional water table is dropping. Well location, aquifer, season, and measurement conditions matter. A buyer should obtain the actual static level for the subject well and understand how it was measured.

sections.heading: Capulin’s permit history reaches back decades
sections.html:
Capulin-area permit records begin in the 1950s, with 27 permits issued during that decade. The record shows 17 in the 1960s, 76 in the 1970s, 44 in the 1980s, 96 in the 1990s, 115 in the 2000s, 56 in the 2010s, and 34 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2026.

The most active drillers named in these records are Heersink Drilling, also listed as Heersink, Scott, with 44 wells; Valley Pump Company, listed as Self, Clinton L., with 31; and Larry Burk Drilling, listed as Burk, Larry, with 28. Those names show local permit history, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, insurance, availability, and references before hiring anyone.

sections.heading: A median-depth Capulin well starts around $10,300 finished
sections.html:
For mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground near Capulin, the local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 86-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $4,300 to $6,400. A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $10,300 to $18,400.

That range is a planning figure, not a guaranteed proposal. The final price can change when the hole must go deeper, when access is difficult, or when the site needs additional trenching or electrical work. Get the bid in writing and ask what happens if the first target depth does not produce enough water. Also separate well costs from septic, driveway, house-site, and other construction work.

sections.heading: Check water quality, dry-hole risk, and the building layout
sections.html:
The mapped environmental record within about 10 miles includes 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site, with 0 historic mine features and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not establish the quality of water at a specific parcel. Test the well for the contaminants relevant to the location and intended use, and review nearby land uses and septic systems.

Low yield and dry holes remain practical risks, especially where permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. The records name 422 wells in that category, 64 in the Unconfined San Luis Vall, and 37 in the Confined San Luis Valley. No Denver Basin aquifer wells appear in the records. Setbacks, casing, grout, septic placement, drainage, and access for a large drilling rig should be checked before finalizing a house site.

sections.heading: Use the records before buying near La Jara or Romeo
sections.html:
Start with the nearest permitted wells, not a countywide assumption. Compare their depths, reported yields, static levels, aquifer descriptions, construction dates, and intended uses. The area’s records are mostly domestic or household permits at 74%, with stock use at 38% and irrigation at 13%; some wells have more than one use. A household-use well is subject to its permit conditions, and Colorado rules commonly limit exempt-well pumping to 35 gallons per minute.

Ask the seller for the permit, construction report, pump information, maintenance history, and recent water testing. If you plan livestock, irrigation, or a new home, confirm that the permitted use covers the plan. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for some uses. Check this early with Colorado DWR and a qualified water-rights professional.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Capulin, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Capulin is 86 feet. The middle half runs from 54 to 198 feet. Most are relatively shallow, with 54% under 100 feet, but the record also includes wells deeper than 600 feet and one reaching 1,044 feet. Your parcel’s aquifer and nearby well records matter more than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Capulin?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $75 per foot in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 86-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $4,300 to $6,400. A finished well including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $10,300 to $18,400. A deeper hole or difficult access can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Capulin wells produce?
faq.a: Among 87 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 13.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-eight percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 1% report under 1 gallon per minute, but reported yields are not available for every permitted well and do not guarantee a new well’s performance.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Capulin?
faq.a: The permit map does not establish drinking-water safety for an individual well. Within about 10 miles, there is 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site, with 0 historic mine features and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Have the subject well tested before drinking it, and consider the well’s construction, septic proximity, nearby land uses, and intended household use.

faq.q: Are Capulin water levels getting lower?
faq.a: Reported static water levels had a median of 14 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 62 feet in the 2020s. That suggests deeper recent measurements, but only 28 wells report static levels, and the records do not prove a regional decline. Location, aquifer, season, and testing conditions can affect the comparison. Obtain the current static level for the property.
